summary: Provides a set of guidelines to aid in the secure operation of the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1281 is a statement of shared rules for running the Internet safely. It divides responsibility between the people who use the network, the organisations that operate it and the companies that build the equipment, and it ends with a five-point checklist for any site that runs a network.

questions: what are the internet security guidelines
subtitle: The shared rules that everyone connected to the Internet was asked to follow.

tldr.problem: The Internet had no central management, so nobody could enforce anything, and its users had no shared statement of what counted as acceptable behaviour.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out six guidelines that divide responsibility between users, service providers and vendors, and then explains in detail what each one means in practice.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard. Its own rules are voluntary, and the memo says so plainly, but it argues that joining the Internet is optional and the rules are part of the bargain.

facts.label: Statute named
facts.value: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986, Title 18 U.S.C. section 1030

today: RFC 1281 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its rules were never enforceable in themselves, because they are voluntary, and the memo says so. It stands as the clearest statement the Internet community made in 1991 of who is responsible for what when it comes to security.

sections.title: Why the Internet Needs Rules of Operation
sections.content:
The memo opens by describing what the Internet had become. It had grown significantly and was now quite diverse: its participants included government institutions and agencies, academic and research institutions, commercial network and electronic mail carriers, non-profit research centres and an increasing array of industrial organisations who were primarily users of the technology. Despite that growth, the system was still operated on a purely collaborative basis. Each participating network took responsibility for its own operation, and service providers, private network operators, users and vendors all cooperated to keep the system functioning.

The authors then name the central difficulty. The voluntary nature of the Internet is both its strength and, perhaps, its most fragile aspect. Rules of operation, like rules of etiquette, are voluntary and largely unenforceable, except where they happen to coincide with national laws, and breaking those laws can lead to prosecution. A common set of rules for the successful and increasingly secure operation of the Internet can, at best, be voluntary, because the laws of the various countries are not uniform about data networking.

The argument the memo makes is a bargain. Since joining the Internet is optional, it is fair to argue that any rules of behaviour are part of the price of joining, and that failure to observe them, apart from whatever legal infrastructure exists, are grounds for sanctions.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody runs the Internet from the top, so the rules have to be agreed rather than imposed. The memo argues that this is fair: you can choose whether to join, and the rules of the house come with the invitation.

sections.title: Who These Guidelines Cover
sections.content:
The guidelines address the entire Internet community: users, hosts, local, regional, domestic and international backbone networks, and the vendors who supply operating systems, routers, network management tools, workstations and other network components.

The memo also fixes what the word security means here, and it is broader than encryption. Security is understood to include protection of the privacy of information, protection of information against unauthorised modification, protection of systems against denial of service, and protection of systems against unauthorised access.

What follows is six main points, stated first in a short list and then elaborated one by one. A bibliography of computer and network security related documents closes the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules apply to everyone on the Internet, from a person at a terminal to the company that sells the routers. Security here means four things: keeping information private, keeping it from being changed without permission, keeping the system available, and keeping unauthorised people out.

sections.title: The Six Guidelines
sections.content: The six guidelines are stated as follows. Users are individually responsible for understanding and respecting the security policies of the systems, both the computers and the networks, that they are using, and are individually accountable for their own behaviour. Users have a responsibility to employ available security mechanisms and procedures for protecting their own data, and a responsibility to assist in protecting the systems they use. Computer and network service providers are responsible for maintaining the security of the systems they operate, and for notifying users of their security policies and of any changes to those policies. Vendors and system developers are responsible for providing systems that are sound and that embody adequate security controls. Users, service providers and hardware and software vendors are responsible for cooperating to provide security. And technical improvements in Internet security protocols should be sought on a continuing basis, with the people who develop new protocols, hardware or software expected to include security considerations as part of the design and development process.
sections.plainLanguage: The six guidelines split into three duties for people, three duties for organisations, and one duty to keep improving the technology. Nobody is asked to do everything on their own.

sections.title: What the Guidelines Mean for Users
sections.content:
The first guideline is elaborated into a statement of personal responsibility. Users are responsible for their own behaviour, and weaknesses in the security of a system are not a licence to penetrate or abuse that system. Users are expected to know the security policies of the computers and networks they access and to stick to them. One clear consequence is that unauthorised access to a computer, or use of a network, is explicitly a violation of the rules of conduct of the Internet, no matter how weak the protection of that computer or network happens to be.

There is a legal dimension. There is growing international attention to legal prohibition against unauthorised access to computer systems, and several countries have recently passed legislation in the area, with the United Kingdom and Australia named. In the United States, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986, Title 18 U.S.C. section 1030, makes it a crime in certain situations to access a Federal interest computer without authorisation, meaning federal government computers, financial institution computers, and a computer that is one of two or more computers used in committing the offence, not all of which are located in the same state. Most of the 50 states in the United States have similar laws.

Users are also individually responsible for all use of the resources assigned to them, so sharing of accounts and of access is strongly discouraged, although the specific rules are necessarily a local matter because access is assigned by individual sites and network operators. The second guideline asks users to handle account privileges responsibly and to follow site procedures. For systems that rely on password protection, users should select good passwords and change them periodically. Proper use of file protection mechanisms, such as access control lists, to define and maintain appropriate file access control is also part of this responsibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Users are told to follow the rules of the site they are on, and not to take advantage of weak security. The memo is clear that a poorly protected machine is still off limits, and it notes that several countries now have laws against unauthorised access.

sections.title: What Service Providers and Vendors Are Expected to Do
sections.content:
Service providers are told that they are responsible for maintaining the security of the systems they operate and for telling users their security policies and any changes to them. A provider may manage resources on behalf of users inside an organisation, such as a university providing network and computer services, or serve a larger external community, such as a regional network provider. Those resources may include host computers used by people, routers, terminal servers, personal computers and other devices that have access to the Internet.

The reason responsibility rests with the owners and operators of these components is that the Internet itself is neither centrally managed nor operated. Even if there were a central authority for the infrastructure, security would still belong to the owners and operators of the systems that hold the primary data and processing resources.

The memo is honest about the trade-offs. Stringent security measures at a site come at the cost of ease of use, since they may complicate how people reach the Internet. A site that chooses to operate an unprotected, open system may be providing a platform for attacks on other Internet hosts while concealing the attacker's identity. Sites that do operate open systems are nonetheless responsible for the behaviour of their users and should be prepared to render assistance to other sites when needed. Wherever possible, sites should try to ensure authenticated Internet access. Sites are encouraged to develop security policies and to communicate them clearly to users and subscribers, and the memo points to the Site Security Handbook, FYI 8, RFC 1244, for guidance on writing good security policies and procedures at both site and network level.

Vendors and system developers have their own duties. Each system should be evaluated in terms of security controls before it is introduced to the Internet community, and each product, whether sold or freely distributed, should describe the security features it incorporates. Vendors have an obligation to repair flaws in the security relevant parts of the systems they sell or give away for Internet use, and they are expected to cooperate with the community in establishing mechanisms for reporting security flaws and in making security-related fixes available in a timely fashion.
sections.plainLanguage: Organisations that run networks are told to keep their systems secure, to publish their policies and to help other sites when they are attacked. Companies that sell the equipment are told to test their products for security, to say what protections they include, and to fix the holes they find.

sections.title: Cooperating, Improving the Protocols, and the Local Checklist
sections.content:
The fifth guideline is about cooperation. The culture and practice of the Internet is to render assistance in security matters to other sites and networks. Each site is expected to notify other sites if it detects a penetration in progress elsewhere, and all sites are expected to help one another respond to security violations, which may include tracing connections, tracking violators and assisting law enforcement efforts. The memo recognises the trade-off between securing a site quickly and leaving it open in the hope of catching the person responsible, and the dilemma between limiting knowledge of a breach and admitting it happened. It does not dictate that a site must expose either its system or its reputation, but encourages sites to render as much assistance as they can.

The sixth guideline adds that technical advances matter too, because existing protocols and operating systems do not provide the level of security that is wanted and feasible at the time. Three kinds of advance are encouraged: improving the basic security mechanisms already in place, with password security described as generally poor throughout the Internet and the user population expanding to include a larger percentage of technically unsophisticated users, so that security defaults on delivered systems must suit them; adding security extensions to the protocol suite, naming network management, routing, file transfer, telnet and mail as the protocols that should be augmented; and improving the design and implementation of operating systems so that they place more emphasis on security.

Appendix A lists five areas that should be addressed in improving local security. There must be a clear statement of the local security policy, communicated to users and available at all times. Adequate security controls must be implemented, which at a minimum means controlling access with passwords, instituting sound password management, and configuring the system to protect itself and the information in it. There must be a capability to monitor security compliance and respond to incidents, with logs of logins, attempted logins and other security-relevant events strongly advised, regular audits of those logs, and a well thought out and published policy about what information is gathered, who has access to it and for what purposes, keeping the privacy of network users in mind. There must be an established chain of communication and control, with a responsible person identified as the security contact, reachable through public directories and pre-authorised to act. And sites and networks that are notified of security incidents should respond in a timely and effective manner, because a site cannot be considered to have good security if it does not respond to incidents quickly, and should install fixes as they become available.

The Security Considerations section says one thing: if security considerations had not been so widely ignored in the Internet, this memo would not have been possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites are asked to help each other when one of them is attacked, and the protocol makers are asked to keep building security into the design. The appendix turns the advice into a five-point checklist for any organisation running a network, ending with the rule that a site which does not respond quickly to a security incident does not have good security.

items.title: Users respect site policy
items.text: Users are individually responsible for understanding and respecting the security policies of the systems they use, and accountable for their own behaviour.

items.title: Users protect their data
items.text: Users must employ the available security mechanisms and procedures for protecting their own data, and assist in protecting the systems they use.

items.title: Providers maintain security
items.text: Computer and network service providers maintain the security of the systems they operate and notify users of their policies and any changes.

items.title: Vendors build sound systems
items.text: Vendors and system developers provide systems which are sound and which embody adequate security controls.

items.title: Everybody cooperates
items.text: Users, service providers and hardware and software vendors are responsible for cooperating to provide security.

items.title: Security is designed in
items.text: Protocols, hardware and software for the Internet are expected to include security considerations as part of the design and development process.

viz.caption: THE FIVE AREAS FOR LOCAL SECURITY FROM APPENDIX A

cells: A clear statement of the local policy, communicated to users, on file and available to them at all times.
At a minimum, password-based access control, sound password management, and configuration that protects the system and its information.
Logs of logins, attempted logins and other security-relevant events, regular audits, and a published policy on what is gathered and who may see it.
A named responsible person, reachable through public directories, familiar with the site's systems and pre-authorised to act.
A timely and effective response to notifications of incidents, and installation of fixes as they become available.
